domains.name: Number Sense & Estimation
subtopics: Place value and magnitude
Read, compose and compare whole numbers and decimals by place value; use powers of ten to explain magnitude.
Compare 4,080 and 4,008 by examining the hundreds and tens places.
A common error is treating 0 as having no structural role; in 4,080 it preserves the tens place.
Estimate sums and products before calculating exactly; reject answers whose size is impossible.
Rounding and estimation
Round integers and decimals to stated place values and use estimation to predict reasonable answers.
Round 7,496 to the nearest hundred: 7,500 because the tens digit is 9.
When estimating 398×21, use 400×20=8,000 as a reasonableness benchmark.
Use compatible numbers, bounds and reverse checks to verify numerical answers.
Factors, multiples and primes
Identify factors, multiples, primes, composite numbers, common factors and common multiples.
For 36, factor pairs are 1×36, 2×18, 3×12 and 4×9.
A number divisible by 6 must be divisible by both 2 and 3.
Apply divisibility rules, prime factorisation, GCD and LCM in unfamiliar problems.
Mental calculation strategies
Choose efficient mental methods for addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and percentage calculations.
Use 25×16 as 100÷4×16=400 rather than repeated addition.
Watch for carrying and place-value errors when splitting numbers mentally.
Select a method, estimate first, calculate, then verify using an inverse operation.
Number properties and puzzles
Use parity, divisibility, remainders and numerical structure to solve non-routine problems.
If an integer is odd, adding another odd integer produces an even result.
A remainder must be smaller than the divisor; this gives an immediate validity check.
Combine parity and divisibility constraints to eliminate impossible cases before calculation.

domains.name: Fractions, Ratios & Proportion
subtopics: Equivalent fractions and simplification
Generate equivalent fractions, reduce fractions using common factors, and compare fractions reliably.
3/4 and 9/12 represent the same quantity because both simplify to 3/4.
Do not compare denominators alone; convert to common denominators or benchmark against 1/2 and 1.
Solve comparison and ordering problems involving mixed numbers and improper fractions.
Fraction operations
Add, subtract, multiply and divide fractions while explaining why each operation works.
For 2/3+1/6, rewrite 2/3 as 4/6, giving 5/6.
Division by a fraction asks how many groups of that size fit into the dividend.
Use inverse operations and magnitude estimates to detect impossible fraction results.
Ratios and equivalent ratios
Interpret ratios as comparisons and scale them without changing the underlying relationship.
A 2:3 ratio becomes 8:12 when both parts are multiplied by 4.
A ratio is not automatically a fraction of the whole; distinguish comparison from total share.
Solve missing-value, mixture and scale problems using tables, unit rates or equivalent ratios.
Proportion and scaling
Recognise proportional relationships and apply scale factors to quantities, diagrams and rates.
If 3 notebooks cost ₹90, the unit price is ₹30 and 7 cost ₹210 under the same rate.
A proportional relationship keeps the same multiplicative scale factor.
Test whether a relationship is truly proportional before applying cross-multiplication.
Percentages in context
Convert between fractions, decimals and percentages and apply percentage change to real situations.
15% of ₹800 is ₹120, so the discounted price is ₹680.
A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease does not return to the starting value.
Solve discount, tax, comparison and percentage-change problems with explicit base quantities.

domains.name: Algebraic Reasoning
subtopics: Variables and expressions
Represent unknown quantities with variables and translate verbal descriptions into algebraic expressions.
Five more than x is x+5; five times x is 5x.
Do not confuse addition with multiplication when translating phrases.
Evaluate expressions for given values and explain the role of each term.
Simplifying expressions
Combine like terms and use distributive reasoning to simplify algebraic expressions.
3x+5x becomes 8x because both terms contain the same variable quantity.
2(x+3) means two groups of both x and 3, so it becomes 2x+6.
Check simplification by substituting a numerical value for x before and after.
Equations and unknowns
Solve one- and multi-step equations while preserving equality.
For 3x+5=20, subtract 5 then divide by 3 to obtain x=5.
Performing the same operation on both sides preserves equality.
Substitute the solution back into the original equation to verify it.
Inequalities and constraints
Interpret inequality symbols and solve simple constrained problems.
x>4 includes every number greater than 4, not 4 itself.
Boundary values determine whether an inequality is strict or inclusive.
Translate word constraints into inequalities and test candidate values.
Algebraic word problems
Build equations from real situations involving unknowns, rates, totals and comparisons.
If three equal notebooks and a ₹20 pen cost ₹140, represent the notebook price as x and solve 3x+20=140.
Identify the unknown and units before writing the equation.
Check the solution against the original story, including units and non-negative constraints.
